title: Gamjatang
subtitle: Spicy pork bone and potato soup
excerpt: Gamjatang is a Korean soup of pork neck bones and potatoes simmered for 90 minutes in a deeply spiced broth of gochugaru, doenjang, and garlic. It serves 4 and is one of the most robustly flavoured soups in Korean cooking. The meat clings to the bones and falls away with light pressure.
sourceNotes: Gamjatang is thought to have originated in Korean labourers' food culture, providing an inexpensive and filling meal from pork bones that were otherwise discarded. Some food historians note that gamja in old regional dialects may refer to the pork spine rather than potato, suggesting the dish may be named for the cut rather than the vegetable. It is now a standard on Korean restaurant menus and a beloved cold-weather home dish.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 2 months without the potatoes, which become grainy after freezing. Add fresh potatoes when reheating.

glossaryTerms.definition: Gamjatang breaks down as gamja (potato in modern Korean, though some historians argue it originally referred to the pork spine in regional dialects) and tang (soup or broth). The dish is defined by its combination of pork bones, potato, and a fiercely spiced red broth. It is one of the heartiest soups in the Korean repertoire and is particularly associated with cold weather.

Pork neck bones are the vertebrae and surrounding meat from the neck of the pig. They are inexpensive, gelatin-rich, and deeply flavoured, making them suited to slow-cooked soups and stews. The meat attached to the bones is fibrous and becomes fall-off-the-bone tender with long, slow simmering. They are sold widely in Asian supermarkets and butchers.

simmered slowly until the broth is richly flavoured and the meat pulls away from the bones. Potatoes are added partway through and absorb the spiced broth as they cook. Spinach and spring onions go in at the very end.

Blanch the pork bones before starting the soup. Cover with cold water, bring to the boil, and boil for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse. This removes blood and impurities that would otherwise cloud the broth and add a muddy flavour. The blanching step takes very little time and makes a significant difference to the finished soup.

items.prepNote: pork neck bones or back bones, ask the butcher to cut into 7cm pieces

content.text: Place the pork bones in a large pot and cover with cold water. Bring to the boil and blanch for 5 minutes. Drain, rinse the bones under cold water, and clean the pot.
Return the bones to the clean pot. Add 2 litres of cold water, the garlic, ginger, doenjang, gochugaru, and soy sauce. Stir well.
Bring to the boil, skimming off any foam. Reduce the heat to a steady simmer, cover, and cook for 50 minutes.
Add the potatoes. Cover and continue simmering for a further 30 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the meat is pulling away from the bones.
Add the spinach and spring onions. Cook uncovered for 5 minutes.
Taste and adjust seasoning with soy sauce. Stir in the sesame oil. Serve in deep bowls with steamed rice.

items.symptom: The broth is cloudy and has an off smell
items.cause: The bones were not blanched before the main cook
items.fix: The blanching step cannot be skipped. If the broth is already cloudy, skim the surface carefully and discard any foam, then continue simmering

items.symptom: The meat is still tough and not releasing from the bone
items.cause: Pork neck bones need at least 80 minutes of simmering to become tender
items.fix: Cover and continue simmering for another 20 to 30 minutes. The meat is ready when it pulls away easily with a spoon

items.symptom: The potatoes are falling apart and thickening the broth
items.cause: They were added too early or cut too small
items.fix: Cut potatoes into large quarters and add them only in the last 30 minutes. If already overcooked, skim out the pieces and stir the broth to incorporate the starch

content.text: Gamjatang is a winter soup and a late-night eating-out dish in Korea. Many gamjatang restaurants are open around the clock, serving as a destination for workers finishing late shifts or people wanting something warming and substantial after a night out. The soup is typically served in a stone pot that keeps the broth boiling at the table. The diner picks the meat from the bones between bites of rice and potato. It is deeply satisfying in a way that only long-simmered bone-based soups can be.
